project_scope.note: Built around gum bumelia morphology and comparison to Texas persimmon and hollies.

family_diagnostics.where_to_look_first: Start with a woody plant bearing alternate entire leaves and sticky/milky latex when naturally exposed, then inspect tiny axillary flower clusters.
family_diagnostics.flower: Small fused radial corolla; in Sideroxylon fertile stamens stand opposite corolla lobes and alternate with petaloid staminodes.
family_diagnostics.fruit: Fleshy berry-like fruit with a hard glossy seed.
family_diagnostics.field_tip: Latex + tiny axillary flowers + glossy hard seed is the local combination.

visual_lesson.teaching_order: whole plant → high-value structure → reproductive confirmation → tie-breaker
visual_lesson.intro: Sideroxylon looks ordinary until you notice the latex, tiny axillary flowers, and the surprisingly hard glossy seed inside the fruit.

steps.title: 1 · Learn the woody/leaf/fruit gestalt
steps.look_for: Woody habit with alternate entire leaves and dark fleshy fruit.
steps.why_it_matters: Sets the family context before close floral anatomy.

steps.title: 2 · Inspect a second plant detail
steps.look_for: Leaf texture, pubescence and armed/unarmed twig variation.

steps.title: 3 · Find the latex only when already exposed
steps.look_for: Sticky/milky latex from existing damage rather than intentionally injuring the plant.
steps.why_it_matters: Latex is a strong supporting family cue.

steps.title: 4 · Read the flower center
steps.look_for: Fertile stamens opposite corolla lobes, alternating with petaloid staminodes.
steps.why_it_matters: This is the precise Sideroxylon floral confirmation.

comparisons.title: Sapotaceae vs Ebenaceae
comparisons.rule: Sapotaceae often has milky/sticky latex and a hard glossy seed; Diospyros lacks that local latex cue and has a conspicuous persistent calyx.

comparisons.title: Sapotaceae vs Aquifoliaceae
comparisons.rule: Ilex has small drupes with several pyrenes; local Sideroxylon commonly has one large hard glossy seed.

visual_lesson.caveat: Do not injure a plant solely to test latex; use existing breaks or fruit where possible.
